questions.text: Science is best described as
options: a way to understand the natural world through observation and experiment
a list of facts to memorise from books
an old story passed from one generation to another
a hobby that has nothing to do with daily life
questions.answer: a way to understand the natural world through observation and experiment
questions.explanation: Science is a systematic way of understanding the natural world through observation, questioning, and experiment.

questions.text: Which of these is the FIRST step that a scientist usually takes?
questions.explanation: All scientific work begins with careful observation of what is happening.

questions.text: The branch of science that mainly studies living things is
questions.explanation: Biology is the study of living organisms — plants, animals, microbes.

questions.text: The branch of science that studies forces, motion, light and electricity is
questions.explanation: Physics deals with matter and energy, including motion, force, light, sound, and electricity.

questions.text: The branch of science that studies substances and the changes they go through is
questions.explanation: Chemistry is the study of substances, their properties, and the changes they undergo.

questions.text: The branch of science that studies stars, planets and other bodies in space is
questions.explanation: Astronomy is the study of celestial objects like stars, planets, and galaxies.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of doing science in daily life?
options: Noticing why ice melts faster on a hot day
questions.answer: Noticing why ice melts faster on a hot day
questions.explanation: Observing and asking why something happens — like ice melting faster when warm — is doing science.

questions.text: Curiosity in science means
options: asking questions about how and why things happen
questions.answer: asking questions about how and why things happen
questions.explanation: Curiosity is the urge to ask questions about the world; it is the engine of science.

questions.text: A hypothesis is best described as
options: a wild guess with no thought
a careful explanation that can be tested
questions.answer: a careful explanation that can be tested
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a thoughtful, testable explanation for an observation.

questions.text: Why do scientists test their ideas with experiments?
options: To make the work look hard
To check whether their idea agrees with the real world
Because their teacher told them to
questions.answer: To check whether their idea agrees with the real world
questions.explanation: Experiments allow ideas (hypotheses) to be checked against actual evidence.

questions.text: In the scientific method, after observing something interesting, the next step is to
questions.explanation: After observation, scientists pose a focused question that can be investigated.

questions.text: Which of these tools helps a scientist measure length?
questions.explanation: A scale or ruler is the basic tool for measuring length.

questions.text: Which of these tools is used to measure temperature?
questions.explanation: A thermometer is used to measure temperature.

questions.text: Which of these tools is used to measure mass?
questions.explanation: A beam balance compares masses to find an object's mass.

questions.text: Riya wants to find out which of two soils holds more water. The MOST scientific approach would be to
options: guess by looking at the colour
pour equal water into equal amounts of each soil and see how much drains out
ask a friend for an answer
memorise an answer from a book
questions.answer: pour equal water into equal amounts of each soil and see how much drains out
questions.explanation: A fair test means changing one variable (the soil) while keeping others equal.

questions.text: Aman observes that wet clothes dry faster on a windy day. The BEST scientific question he can ask is
options: Does wind speed up evaporation of water?
questions.answer: Does wind speed up evaporation of water?
questions.explanation: A good scientific question is focused, testable, and connected to the observation.

questions.text: Two students measure the same pencil. One says 13 cm, the other says 15 cm. The most likely reason is that
options: one of them did not place the zero of the scale at the end of the pencil
questions.answer: one of them did not place the zero of the scale at the end of the pencil
questions.explanation: Different readings on the same object usually mean a measurement error, often misalignment of zero.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a part of doing science?
options: Believing whatever you wish without checking
questions.answer: Believing whatever you wish without checking
questions.explanation: Science requires evidence; belief without checking is not science.

questions.text: A student finds that her plant grew taller in two weeks. To CONCLUDE that fertiliser caused the growth, she would also need
options: a similar plant of the same kind not given fertiliser, kept in the same conditions
another plant that grew in different soil with different sunlight
questions.answer: a similar plant of the same kind not given fertiliser, kept in the same conditions
questions.explanation: A control plant under matched conditions lets you separate the fertiliser's effect from other factors.

questions.text: In an experiment, the variable that you deliberately change is called the
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose to see the effect.

questions.text: Which is the BEST way to be sure of a scientific result?
options: Do the experiment once and trust it
Repeat the experiment several times and check that the results are consistent
Believe the first answer that comes to mind
questions.answer: Repeat the experiment several times and check that the results are consistent
questions.explanation: Repeating an experiment and checking consistency reduces the chance that a result was due to error or chance.

questions.text: A scientist's notebook is important because
options: it makes the table look full
it allows others to check, repeat, and trust the work
it is required to be heavy
questions.answer: it allows others to check, repeat, and trust the work
questions.explanation: Honest, detailed records let other scientists verify and build on the work.

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST example of a scientific question?
options: Does adding salt change the time it takes water to boil?
questions.answer: Does adding salt change the time it takes water to boil?
questions.explanation: A scientific question can be tested with measurement and a fair experiment.

questions.text: The school football is missing. The MOST scientific way to find it is to
options: trace where it was last used and check those places one by one
questions.answer: trace where it was last used and check those places one by one
questions.explanation: Using observation and a logical search is applying the scientific way of thinking to daily life.

questions.text: Which person used science to make life better in India?
options: A character in a fairy tale
Sir C. V. Raman, who studied light
questions.answer: Sir C. V. Raman, who studied light
questions.explanation: C. V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in physics for his work on the scattering of light.

questions.text: Science begins with careful observation.
questions.explanation: Observation is the very first step of the scientific method.

questions.text: Physics is the study of living organisms.
questions.explanation: Biology studies living organisms; physics studies forces, motion, light, and electricity.

questions.text: Curiosity helps a scientist ask better questions.
questions.explanation: Curiosity drives scientists to ask 'why' and 'how' about what they observe.

questions.text: In a fair test you should change as many things as possible at the same time.
questions.explanation: In a fair test you change only one variable at a time, keeping others the same.

questions.text: A hypothesis is a guess that can be tested.
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable, thoughtful explanation for an observation.

questions.text: Repeating an experiment many times helps make the result more reliable.
questions.explanation: Repetition reveals whether the first result was consistent or due to chance.

questions.text: Astronomy is the branch of science that studies stars and planets.
questions.explanation: Astronomy studies celestial bodies like stars, planets, and galaxies.

questions.text: To compare which detergent cleans cloth better, you should use the same kind of cloth and same dirt for both detergents.
questions.explanation: A fair test keeps everything else the same and changes only the variable being tested.

questions.text: A scientist should accept any explanation given by an elder, even without checking.
questions.explanation: In science, claims are checked against evidence, no matter who said them.

questions.text: If two scientists doing the same experiment carefully get different results, the disagreement should be ignored.
questions.explanation: Differences should be investigated; that is how science makes progress.

questions.text: Recording observations honestly, even when they don't match the expected answer, is essential in science.
questions.explanation: Honesty in recording is a core value of science. Surprises often lead to discoveries.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of science that studies forces, motion, and energy.
questions.explanation: Physics studies matter and energy, including forces, motion, and light.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of science that studies substances and the changes they undergo.
questions.explanation: Chemistry studies substances and how they change.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of science that studies living organisms.
questions.explanation: Biology is the study of life — plants, animals, microbes.

questions.text: In the scientific method, after observation comes asking a _____.
questions.explanation: A focused question turns curiosity into something testable.

questions.text: A testable explanation for an observation is called a _____.
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a careful, testable answer to a scientific question.

questions.text: In a fair test, only _____ thing should be changed at a time.
questions.explanation: Changing only one variable lets us pin the effect on that variable.

questions.text: The instrument used to measure mass is called a _____.
questions.explanation: A beam balance compares unknown masses with known masses.

questions.text: The drive to ask questions and explore the world around us is called _____.
questions.explanation: Curiosity is the urge to find out 'why' and 'how' about what we see.

questions.text: To check whether two batteries last the same time, you must use the same _____ for both batteries.
questions.explanation: Same device, same setting — only the battery should change to make the test fair.

questions.text: In an experiment, the variable measured to see the effect is called the _____ variable.
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what changes in response to the independent variable.

questions.text: The variable that the scientist deliberately changes is called the _____ variable.
questions.explanation: The independent variable is set by the experimenter to test its effect.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of science that studies stars, planets, and galaxies.
questions.explanation: Astronomy studies celestial bodies and the universe.

questions.text: In one or two sentences, explain what science is.
questions.answer: Science is a way of learning about the natural world by careful observation, asking questions, testing ideas, and sharing what we find with others.
questions.explanation: A short, student-friendly definition that captures observation, questioning, testing, and sharing.

questions.text: Name any three branches of science.
questions.answer: Physics, Chemistry, Biology. (Other valid answers include Astronomy, Geology, Botany, Zoology.)
questions.explanation: Any three of physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, geology, etc. are correct.

questions.text: Write the steps of the scientific method in order.
questions.answer: Observe, ask a question, form a hypothesis, test the hypothesis with an experiment, record and analyse the results, draw a conclusion, and share the findings.
questions.explanation: This is the standard sequence of steps in scientific inquiry.

questions.text: Give one example of doing science in daily life.
questions.answer: Sample answer: noticing that a cake takes longer to bake on a rainy day, asking why, and trying the same recipe on a sunny day to compare. Any answer that involves observation + question + checking is acceptable.
questions.explanation: The student should describe an everyday observation and a way to check it.

questions.text: Why is curiosity important for a scientist?
questions.answer: Curiosity makes a scientist notice unusual things and ask 'why' or 'how'. Without curiosity there would be no question to investigate, and so no science.
questions.explanation: Curiosity is the starting point of scientific work.

questions.text: Two students measure the same plant's height and get 28 cm and 31 cm. Suggest two possible reasons for the difference and how they could resolve it.
questions.answer: Possible reasons: (i) the scale was not placed at the very base of the plant, (ii) the plant was not held straight, or one student rounded their reading. To resolve: each student should measure again with the scale placed exactly at soil level, holding the plant vertical, and they should compare readings until they agree.
questions.explanation: The student should identify causes of measurement error and a way to reduce them.

questions.text: Why is it important to record observations in a notebook?
questions.answer: Recording observations keeps the data exact, helps us notice patterns later, and lets others repeat the work and check whether they get the same results.
questions.explanation: Honest records make the science trustworthy and reproducible.

questions.text: Design a simple fair test to find out whether warm water dissolves sugar faster than cold water. Mention what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would measure.
questions.answer: Take two glasses, one with warm water and one with cold water of the same amount. Add the same spoonful of sugar to each at the same time and stir each at the same speed. Measure the time taken for the sugar to dissolve fully in each. The water temperature is the only thing that changes; everything else stays the same. Compare the two times.
questions.explanation: A clear fair-test design: one variable changed, all others kept identical, time is measured.

questions.text: Imagine you noticed that ants move in a long line in your garden. Plan a small scientific investigation: state your question, your hypothesis, what you would do, what you would measure, and how you would decide whether your hypothesis is supported.
questions.answer: Question: Why do ants move in a line? Hypothesis: Ants follow a chemical 'trail' left by other ants. Plan: Mark a clear trail of ants on the ground with a chalk line so I can find it again. Wipe across the trail with a wet cloth between two points and watch what the ants do for the next ten minutes. Measure: How many ants cross the wiped section directly versus how many wander off looking for the trail. Decision: If most ants get confused at the wiped section and search around, my hypothesis is supported. If they cross straight as if nothing happened, the hypothesis is not supported and I would think of a new explanation, such as the ants following sight or sound.
questions.explanation: Looks for a complete plan: question, hypothesis, method, measurement, and a clear way to decide.

questions.text: Mira sees that her plant grows taller near the window than in the corner. The BEST first step for her is to
options: assume that the corner is haunted
ask whether sunlight near the window is helping the plant
decide all plants need windows and stop thinking
questions.answer: ask whether sunlight near the window is helping the plant
questions.explanation: Forming a focused, testable question is the right first step after observing a difference.

questions.text: The branch of science that studies the Earth, its rocks, and its history is called
questions.explanation: Geology is the study of Earth, its rocks, soils, and the history written in them.

questions.text: Which is NOT a branch of science?
questions.explanation: Astrology is not a science because its claims are not testable. Astronomy is the science of the sky.

questions.text: Which of these activities is NOT science?
options: Watching how seeds sprout in different soils
Measuring how fast a fan cools a room
Making up a story about flying horses
Recording the temperature of milk every minute
questions.answer: Making up a story about flying horses
questions.explanation: Stories from imagination are creative but not based on observation or testing.

questions.text: In any experiment, the parts that you keep the same are called
questions.explanation: Controlled variables (or controls) are the conditions kept the same so they don't affect the result.

questions.text: A student claims that 'all plants need sunlight to grow'. Which observation would BEST challenge this claim?
options: A plant in a sunny garden grew tall
A mushroom grew well in a dark cellar
A plant on a windowsill grew tall
questions.answer: A mushroom grew well in a dark cellar
questions.explanation: Mushrooms (fungi) grow without sunlight, so they're an exception that challenges the broad claim about 'all plants'.

questions.text: You read two reports about a new fertilizer. Report A used three plants for one week. Report B used twenty plants for two months. Which report is more trustworthy and why?
options: Report A, because it was faster
Report B, because it used more plants over more time
Report A, because it had nicer pictures
questions.answer: Report B, because it used more plants over more time
questions.explanation: Larger samples and longer studies usually give more reliable results.

questions.text: You see fewer butterflies in your garden this year. The MOST scientific way to investigate is to
options: assume someone scared them away and stop thinking
compare the number of butterflies counted at the same time each day for a few weeks with last year's notes, and look for differences in flowers, weather, and chemicals used
wait for them to come back
questions.answer: compare the number of butterflies counted at the same time each day for a few weeks with last year's notes, and look for differences in flowers, weather, and chemicals used
questions.explanation: This is observation + careful comparison + considering possible causes — the scientific approach.

questions.text: Which is a good attitude for a scientist?
options: Believing the first answer that comes to mind
Being open to changing one's mind when new evidence appears
questions.answer: Being open to changing one's mind when new evidence appears
questions.explanation: Scientific thinking welcomes new evidence and updates ideas accordingly.

questions.text: You notice that a rubber ball bounces higher when it is warm than when it is cold. The BEST scientific question is
options: Does temperature change how high a ball bounces?
questions.answer: Does temperature change how high a ball bounces?
questions.explanation: It is focused, testable, and connects directly to the observation.

questions.text: Which person is associated with the laws of motion?
questions.explanation: Newton stated the three laws of motion in his work in the 17th century.

questions.text: Marie Curie is famous in science for
questions.explanation: Marie Curie studied radioactivity and won two Nobel Prizes.

questions.text: Which of these statements BEST describes how science grows?
options: Once an answer is found, it never changes
Each new careful experiment can confirm, refine, or even change earlier answers
Science depends on a single book of rules
questions.answer: Each new careful experiment can confirm, refine, or even change earlier answers
questions.explanation: Science is self-correcting: new evidence can update or replace older ideas.

questions.text: To compare how fast different paper shapes fall, you should drop them
options: from the same height at the same time
questions.answer: from the same height at the same time
questions.explanation: Same height and same release time make the comparison fair.

questions.text: A friend says, 'Cold water freezes faster if you boil it first.' To check this, you should
options: run an experiment with two identical containers, one with previously boiled water and one with regular water, both placed in the same freezer at the same time
questions.answer: run an experiment with two identical containers, one with previously boiled water and one with regular water, both placed in the same freezer at the same time
questions.explanation: Testing claims with a fair experiment is the scientific approach.

questions.text: Geology is the study of stars and galaxies.
questions.explanation: Geology studies Earth and its rocks; astronomy studies stars and galaxies.

questions.text: Asking 'How does this work?' is a scientific way of thinking.
questions.explanation: Asking 'how' or 'why' about something is the start of scientific thinking.

questions.text: In an experiment, you should change only the variable you want to test.
questions.explanation: Changing one variable at a time keeps the test fair.

questions.text: Asking questions in class is a sign that you don't understand and should be avoided.
questions.explanation: Asking questions is exactly what curious, scientific minds do.

questions.text: Botany is a branch of biology that studies plants.
questions.explanation: Botany is the branch of biology that focuses on plants.

questions.text: A correlation between two events always means that one causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation does not equal causation; both could be due to a third factor or just chance.

questions.text: _____ is the careful, repeated activity by which scientists test their ideas.
questions.explanation: An experiment is a controlled procedure used to test a hypothesis.

questions.text: The variables in an experiment that are kept the same to make the test fair are called _____ variables.
questions.explanation: Controlled variables don't change so they don't affect the result.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of biology that studies animals.
questions.explanation: Zoology is the branch of biology dealing with animals.

questions.text: _____ is the branch of biology that studies plants.
questions.explanation: Botany is the branch of biology focused on plants.

questions.text: To find out whether a fertilizer helps plant growth, the plant given fertilizer should be compared with a similar plant in the same conditions but without fertilizer; the second plant is called the _____ plant.
questions.explanation: A control matches the conditions without the variable being tested.

questions.text: Give two examples of careful observation in daily life.
questions.answer: Sample answers: noticing that ice cream melts faster on a hot day; noticing that a tap drips faster after the gasket has worn out. Any two clear daily observations are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Tests whether the student can spot observations beyond a textbook context.

questions.text: How is asking a scientific question different from asking just any question?
questions.answer: A scientific question is focused, has a clear topic, and can be tested or answered by observing or measuring something. Just any question may be vague, opinion-based, or impossible to test.
questions.explanation: Highlights the testable nature of scientific questions.

questions.text: You want to find out which of two routes to school is faster. Describe a fair test you could run in one week.
questions.answer: Pick the same start time and the same way of moving (walking) for the whole week. Take Route A on three days and Route B on three days, switching days. Use a stopwatch to record how long each trip takes. Compare the average times for each route. Any plan that controls timing and movement and measures duration is acceptable.
questions.explanation: Looks for a clear fair-test plan with one variable changed.

questions.text: What is the purpose of sharing scientific findings with others?
questions.answer: Sharing lets other scientists check the work, repeat the experiment, build on it, or correct it. It is also how knowledge is added to the world for everyone's benefit.
questions.explanation: Sharing is part of how science improves and spreads.

questions.text: A student says, 'My grandfather always says that eating tulsi cures all illnesses, so it must be true.' What is wrong with this reasoning, and how would you check the claim scientifically?
questions.answer: Just because someone respected says it does not make a claim true; in science, evidence matters more than authority. To check, you'd look for careful studies that compare patients given tulsi with similar patients not given tulsi, see what specific illnesses (if any) tulsi helps with, and check whether the result has been confirmed by several studies.
questions.explanation: Tests evidence-based reasoning vs. argument from authority.

questions.text: Choose any everyday observation (for example, why your bicycle squeaks, why a fan slows when dust gathers, or why grass grows greener after rain). Write a small investigation plan with: (a) the observation, (b) a question, (c) a hypothesis, (d) materials and steps for a test, (e) what you'd measure, and (f) how you'd decide whether your hypothesis is supported.
questions.answer: Sample answer using the rain–grass observation. (a) Observation: Grass looks greener after a rainy week. (b) Question: Does extra water make grass produce more green pigment? (c) Hypothesis: Plants given more water grow more green pigment in their leaves. (d) Materials: two same-size grass patches in pots, water, a measuring jug, a sunny spot, a chart. Steps: water Pot A with 200 ml every day; water Pot B with 50 ml every day; keep both in the same sunlight; for two weeks, photograph the leaves and rate their colour on a 1–5 scale. (e) Measure the daily colour rating and the height of the grass. (f) If Pot A is consistently greener and growing more, the hypothesis is supported. If both look the same or B looks greener, the hypothesis is not supported and I'd consider whether soil nutrients matter more than water amount.
questions.explanation: Open-ended; full credit for any well-structured plan with the six listed parts.

questions.text: Some people believe that 'ancient remedies are always better than modern medicines because they are natural.' Discuss this claim from a scientific point of view, mentioning what evidence we should look for before agreeing or disagreeing.
questions.answer: From a scientific point of view, the claim cannot be accepted just because it sounds good. 'Natural' does not automatically mean 'safe' or 'effective' — many strong poisons are natural. Before agreeing or disagreeing, we should ask: Has the remedy been carefully tested in many people? Were the people compared with a similar group not given the remedy? Were the results consistent across studies? Are the doses safe? Some traditional remedies do work and have been confirmed by modern studies, while some do not. The right scientific approach is to test each remedy for the specific illness, not to accept or reject all of them as a group.
questions.explanation: Tests evidence-based evaluation and recognising that 'natural' is not a scientific claim.

questions.text: A scientific result is most reliable when
options: many people repeat it and get the same result
it is told as a story
questions.answer: many people repeat it and get the same result
questions.explanation: Reproducibility — many people getting the same result — is a hallmark of reliable science.

questions.text: Aanya wonders if her father's remedy of eating jaggery for cough really works. To investigate scientifically, she would
options: gather a few people with cough, give half of them jaggery and the other half a piece of sugar candy that looks similar, then track who gets better
conclude immediately that all home remedies work
questions.answer: gather a few people with cough, give half of them jaggery and the other half a piece of sugar candy that looks similar, then track who gets better
questions.explanation: This sets up a comparison group and a fair test, the scientific way to evaluate the claim.

questions.text: Why do scientists use SI units like metre, second, and kilogram?
options: Because they are easier to spell
So scientists everywhere can compare results
questions.answer: So scientists everywhere can compare results
questions.explanation: Standard units allow scientists across the world to share measurements without confusion.

questions.text: Curiosity is one of the most important attitudes in science.
questions.explanation: Curiosity drives the questions scientists ask.

questions.text: To compare two batteries, you must use the same device and start them at the same time.
questions.explanation: Same device, same time — only the battery changes — is a fair test.

questions.text: In a fair test, the variables that are kept the same are sometimes called the _____ variables.
questions.explanation: Controlled variables are held constant.

questions.text: A claim that cannot be tested by observation or experiment is said to be unscientific because it is not _____.
questions.explanation: Testability is a hallmark of a scientific claim.

questions.text: Which Indian scientist won a Nobel Prize for discovering the scattering of light, and what is the effect named after him?
questions.answer: Sir C. V. Raman, the effect is the Raman Effect.
questions.explanation: Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for the Raman Effect.

questions.text: Working with others on a science project usually
options: leads to better ideas through discussion
questions.answer: leads to better ideas through discussion
questions.explanation: Collaboration brings different views and reduces individual mistakes.

questions.text: A model in science is BEST described as
options: a perfect copy of a real thing
a simpler picture or rule that helps us understand or predict something complex
questions.answer: a simpler picture or rule that helps us understand or predict something complex
questions.explanation: Models simplify reality so we can understand and predict it.

questions.text: A student concludes from one experiment that 'all metals expand on heating'. What is the BEST critique of this conclusion?
options: It is correct, no critique needed
Only one or two metals were tested, so the broad claim about ALL metals is not yet justified
The student should never conclude anything
questions.answer: Only one or two metals were tested, so the broad claim about ALL metals is not yet justified
questions.explanation: A few cases don't justify a universal claim; more samples are needed.

questions.text: You want to know if a magnet attracts a coin. The MOST scientific approach is to
options: bring the magnet close to the coin and see if it sticks
questions.answer: bring the magnet close to the coin and see if it sticks
questions.explanation: Direct test by observation answers the question quickly and reliably.
